title: Elicitation; malicious links and files
goal_html: Students practice two skills: (1) recognizing when a conversation is extracting information through elicitation gambits, and (2) reading URLs and filenames methodically to flag malicious indicators. Ties to LO 1.1.A (identify attack indicators) and 1.1.C (describe delivery vectors for social-engineering attacks).
steps_html:
Part A, URL/file inspection (15 min)

  1. Each pair opens the simulation and works through the message set together, agreeing on every indicator before submitting each entry. They must reach the target score.
  2. For any message they got wrong, each partner writes one sentence explaining the rule they missed, why that indicator applies.

Part B, Elicitation role-play (10 min)

  1. Partner A plays a social engineer trying to find out the name of the company's backup server using only indirect questions (no direct "what is the server called?"). Partner B plays a receptionist who will answer natural conversational questions but should refuse direct requests.
  2. After 4 minutes, partners swap roles. The new attacker tries a different gambit (flattery, wrong-statement, or mutual disclosure).
  3. After both rounds, both partners write: which gambit was used, what information was extracted, and what the receptionist should have done differently.
collaborate_html: After Part B, each pair teams up with another pair. Share the gambits used and compare what information leaked. Discuss: is it possible to have a normal helpful conversation AND protect sensitive details? What is the minimum a receptionist should reveal to a stranger?
exit_html: Each student submits: one URL they find in their (personal, non-school) email that contains at least one indicator from the lesson, or "none found", plus which indicator type and why. (If using school devices, the instructor provides a printed set of sample URLs instead.)
